notes.meaning: News had reached Paul that a man in the church was living with his father's wife. That means his stepmother, in an ongoing relationship, not a single act. The law of Moses forbade this. Even pagans thought it shocking and almost unheard of, so the church's shame was all the greater.

Instead of grieving, the church was proud of itself. Paul is troubled that they shrugged off such a sin. They should have mourned, as if over a death, and put the man out of their fellowship. Church discipline should always start with sorrow, not anger.

Paul was far away, but his heart and attention were with them. The facts were well known, so he had already made up his mind about what must be done. This is not the harsh judging Jesus warned against. It is a faithful leader facing an open sin the church had ignored.

The whole church was to meet together in Jesus' name, and Paul would be with them in spirit. Their authority came from Christ, who promised to be with His gathered people. Even Paul, an apostle, did not act alone. He had the church act together, so that no single person held this power.

The church was to put the man out of its fellowship. This is called excommunication. Outside the church he would no longer stand under Christ's care, and Satan rules there. The goal was not to destroy him but to rescue him, so that he would turn back and be saved when Jesus returns. Later Paul urged the church to welcome a repentant man back (2 Corinthians 2:6-7).

differ.view: Being handed over to Satan simply means being put out of the church. The 'flesh' destroyed is his sinful nature, tamed so he may live for God.
Satan was usually allowed to bring pain or sickness on such an offender, unless he quickly repented.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Chrysostom says Paul 'delivers' the man as one hands a child to a strict teacher. The man might suffer sores or disease like Job, but the devil is kept within limits, and the door to repentance stays open.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Cut off from the church and its sacraments, which protect a believer, the man is open to Satan's physical attacks. That suffering might lead him to repent and be saved.

notes.meaning: Their boasting was out of place while such sin sat among them. Leaven is yeast, like a bit of old sourdough. A little of it spreads through the whole batch of dough. In the same way, one sin left alone can spread and harm the whole church.

Before Passover, Jewish families searched their homes and threw out every bit of leaven. Paul tells the church to clean out sin the same way and to become what they already are in Christ: a fresh, pure batch. Jesus is our Passover Lamb, already sacrificed. That means He died in our place. His death does not make holiness unneeded. It gives us the strongest reason to be holy.

Because Christ has been sacrificed, the whole Christian life is like a joyful, never-ending feast. We are to keep it without the old 'yeast' of ill will and wickedness. Instead we keep it with the pure bread of sincerity and truth, being honest and real inside and out.

Paul had told them in an earlier letter, which most believe is now lost, not to mix closely with sexually immoral people. He did not mean unbelievers in the wider world who are immoral, greedy, cheating, or worship idols. To avoid them entirely you would have to leave the world. Christians must still live, work, and do good among unbelievers.

What Paul meant was this: don't keep close company with someone who calls himself a fellow believer but openly lives in such sins. He names sexual sin, greed, idol worship, abusive speech, drunkenness, and cheating. Sharing a meal was a sign of friendship, so do not even eat with such a person. The aim is to shame him into repenting, still treating him as a brother to be warned, not an enemy.

It is not the church's job to pass sentence on people outside it. God will judge them. But the church is responsible for its own members. So Paul ends with words from the law of Moses: put the wicked man out from among you.
